hints.junior: Every one of 40 apps breaks on the same npm install — a caret range pulls the new major in with no warning and no way to opt in early.
hints.mid: A single v3 tag conflates "the new API exists" with "every consumer is forced onto it right now" — those should be two separate decisions.
hints.staff: A design system with 40 consumers has a blast radius of 40 teams — every major version becomes an org-wide fire drill unless the rollout is decoupled from the version bump.

hints.junior: Watch what happens to all 8 apps the instant hard-cutover v3 goes out, versus migrating them one at a time under the shim.
hints.mid: Staged mode's "Run codemod" button migrates one app off the deprecated prop per click, without touching the other 7.
hints.staff: The staged-mode counter tracks real per-app migration state, the same shape as the real removal criterion: usage telemetry hits zero, not a countdown timer.

hints.junior: First request: 200 OK is not how this works — a shim maps the old prop name to the new one internally so the app keeps running while it gets a warning.
hints.mid: Real systems automate the far side of the deprecation window too — Polaris ships a migrator CLI, Carbon ships an upgrade codemod package, both doing the rename work automatically.
hints.staff: The version number stops being the forcing function — the shim's measured removal criterion (usage telemetry hits zero) is what actually decides when it comes out.

hints.junior: A shim nobody ever removes just becomes a second, permanently-supported API that every future engineer has to learn alongside the real one.
hints.mid: Log every real hit of the shim, not just a console warning a developer might never see — that's the difference between a guess and an actual usage number.
hints.staff: Watch for a dual-package hazard: two major versions of the same design system landing in one app's dependency tree, one direct and one transitive, which a naive bundler won't dedupe.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a design system's version 3 release that broke every single one of forty consuming apps on the same install, all at once, with no warning.
sections.mid: A caret version range means any consuming app pulls in a new major the next time it installs, with no deprecation period and no way to opt in on its own timeline.
sections.staff: The deeper issue is treating a shared design system's release like one team's own deploy, when its actual blast radius is every team that imports it.

sections.junior: Instead of one hard cutover, a safer release keeps the old way of using a component working for a while, and just warns the team that something changed.
sections.mid: A compatibility shim maps the old prop names to the new ones internally, so the public API stays backward compatible during a deprecation window even though the internals changed.
sections.staff: The version number stops being the forcing function. What actually decides when the shim comes out is real usage telemetry hitting zero, not a date on a calendar.

sections.junior: Try switching between a hard cutover and a staged rollout, and watch what happens to the eight simulated apps in each mode.
sections.mid: In staged mode, migrating one app never touches the other seven, that's the whole point of the shim.
sections.staff: Notice the staged mode is tracked by a real per-app counter, not a timer, matching how the actual removal decision gets made.

sections.junior: A shim that keeps the old way working, plus a tool that updates the code automatically, lets every team migrate on its own schedule instead of all at once.
sections.mid: Ship the compatibility layer active by default so a routine install doesn't turn into an outage, and pair it with an automated code migration.
sections.staff: Measure real usage of the shim before removing it, and watch for two versions of the same package ending up in one app's dependency tree at once.
